entry: Law of electrical current and voltage. In an ohmic conductor, the [[Electric current|electric current]] between two points is directly proportional to the [[Voltage|voltage]] across them. The constant of proportionality is the resistance, giving V = IR, or equivalently I = GV, where G is the conductance. The law is an empirical relation that describes the conductivity of most electrically conductive materials over many orders of magnitude of current; materials that do not obey it are called non-ohmic. The law is named after German physicist [[Georg Ohm]], who described his measurements in a treatise published in 1827. [[Henry Cavendish]] had made similar measurements in 1781, but his results were unknown until [[James Clerk Maxwell]] published them in 1879. The vector form, J = σE, is due to [[Gustav Kirchhoff]].

Viscous, water-insoluble liquid. Oils are nonpolar substances composed primarily of [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]]. They are hydrophobic and lipophilic, and most are unsaturated [[Lipid|lipids]] that are liquid at room temperature. Plant and animal oils include fats, which are precursors to [[Soap|soap]] and components of many foods, and drying oils, which are key components of some paints and lacquers. Petroleum-derived oils include distillates from crude oil and shale oil, used as fuels, hydraulic fluids, transformer oil and heat-transfer fluids. Synthetic oils, mainly used as lubricants, are produced from [[Petrochemical|petrochemicals]]. Petroleum-based oils originate from ancient fossilized organisms such as zooplankton and algae. Oil has long been a religious medium, and holy anointing oil has been an important ritual liquid in [[Judaism]] and [[Christianity]].

Experiment to measure the elementary electric charge. Robert A. Millikan and Harvey Fletcher performed it in 1909 in the Ryerson Physical Laboratory at the [[University of Chicago]]. Tiny charged oil droplets were observed between two horizontal metal plates forming a [[Capacitor|capacitor]]. With no field applied, the fall speed of a droplet gave its radius and therefore its mass. A voltage was then adjusted until the drop hung in balance against [[Gravity|gravity]], which gave its charge. Repeated measurements showed that all charges were small integer multiples of a base value, which the researchers proposed as the charge of a single [[Electron|electron]]. Their value, 1.5924(17)×10⁻¹⁹ C, differs by about 0.6% from the currently accepted value of 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C. Millikan won the [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics in 1923, in part because of this experiment. Later revelations that he selectively reported data have not overturned the core findings.

Painting method using [[Pigment|pigments]] bound with drying oil. Oil paint has been the most common technique for artistic painting on [[Canvas|canvas]], wood panel or copper for several centuries. Its advantages include greater flexibility, richer and denser color, the use of layers, and a wider range from light to dark. The oldest known oil paintings were made by Buddhist artists in Afghanistan in the 7th century AD. Europeans had used oil paint on statues and woodwork from at least the 12th century, but its common use for painted images began with Early Netherlandish painting. By the height of the [[Renaissance]], oil had almost completely replaced egg tempera for panel paintings in most of Europe, though not for [[Icon|Orthodox icons]] or wall paintings. Paint is often thinned with [[Turpentine|turpentine]], and the fat-over-lean rule requires each layer to contain more oil than the one below it.

Industrial plant for refining crude oil into fuels and other products. Refineries produce gasoline, diesel fuel, asphalt base, fuel oils, heating oil, [[Kerosene|kerosene]], liquefied petroleum gas and petroleum naphtha. [[Ethylene|Ethylene]] and [[Propylene|propylene]] can also be produced by cracking crude oil directly. Refineries are large complexes of piping and [[Distillation|distillation]] columns and other processing units, and they can be thought of as types of [[Chemical plant|chemical plants]]. In 2020, global refinery capacity was about 101.2 million barrels per day. Since December 2008 the world's largest refinery has been the Jamnagar Refinery, owned by Reliance Industries in [[Gujarat]], [[India]], with a capacity of 1.24 million barrels (197,000 m³) per day. The modern petroleum industry is said to have begun in 1846, when Abraham Gesner of Nova Scotia, Canada, devised a process to produce kerosene from coal.

Organic-rich, fine-grained [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rock]] containing kerogen. Kerogen is a solid mixture of organic compounds from which liquid [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]] can be produced. Heating oil shale to a high temperature causes pyrolysis, which yields a vapor; cooling the vapor separates a liquid called shale oil. Shale oil is a substitute for conventional crude oil, but extracting it costs more, both financially and environmentally. Oil shale can also be burned directly as a low-grade fuel for [[Electricity generation|power generation]] and district heating. A 2016 estimate put global resources at 6.05 trillion barrels (962 billion cubic meters) of oil in place. Only [[Estonia]] and China have well-established oil shale industries. Mining and processing raise concerns over land use, waste disposal, water use, [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse-gas]] emissions and air pollution. Oil shale differs from oil-bearing shales, such as the Bakken Formation, which contain tight oil.

Drillhole in the Earth designed to bring [[Petroleum|petroleum]] to the surface. Usually some [[Natural gas|natural gas]] is released along with the oil, and a well designed to produce only gas may be called a gas well. Creating a well costs at least hundreds of thousands of dollars, and much more in difficult locations, such as offshore. Wells are often sold between companies as assets, because a low-output well can become valuable when prices rise. Techniques such as hydraulic fracturing have made some wells viable. Neglected or abandoned wells can leak methane and other toxic substances, and a 2020 Reuters estimate counted at least 29 million abandoned wells internationally. The earliest known oil wells were drilled in China in AD 347, using bits attached to [[Bamboo|bamboo]] poles. In the United States the petroleum industry began in 1859, when Edwin Drake found oil near Titusville, [[Pennsylvania]].

Anishinaabe people of the [[Great Lakes]] region and northern plains. The Ojibwe population is about 320,000, with 170,742 in the United States as of 2010 and about 160,000 in Canada. Their language, Anishinaabemowin, belongs to the Algonquian family. They are known for [[Canoe|birchbark canoes]], birchbark scrolls, [[Copper|copper]] mining and trade, and the harvesting of wild rice and maple syrup. Their Midewiwin Society keeps detailed scrolls of oral history, songs, maps and other knowledge. The dreamcatcher originated among the Ojibwe. European powers, Canada and the U.S. colonized Ojibwe lands, and many settlers moved onto their ancestral territory.

Striped forest mammal (*Okapia johnstoni*) endemic to northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Along with the [[Giraffe|giraffe]], it is the only living member of the family Giraffidae. Its coat is chocolate to reddish brown, with white horizontal stripes on the legs, and males have short ossicones. It stands about 1.5 m tall and weighs 200 to 350 kg. A [[Herbivore|herbivore]], it eats leaves, buds, grasses, ferns, fruits and fungi, and is essentially solitary in canopy forests. The okapi is classified as endangered on the IUCN Red List. Threats include logging, human settlement, mining and hunting for bushmeat and skin.

Largest of the Okinawa Islands, in the [[Ryukyu Islands]] of Japan. The island is about 106 km long and has an area of 1,206.98 sq km. Its population was 1,384,762 in 2009. The city of Naha, seat of [[Okinawa Prefecture]], lies on its southwestern part. After the [[Battle of Okinawa]] in 1945, the United States administered the island until 1972, and about 26,000 [[United States Armed Forces|U.S. military]] personnel are stationed there today. U.S. installations cover about 25% of the island, a point of contention for locals. Crimes by U.S. personnel, including the 1995 Okinawa rape incident, have prompted protests.

Southernmost and westernmost prefecture of Japan. It consists of the Okinawa, Sakishima and Daitō island groups, spread about 1,000 km east to west. Of its 160 islands, 49 are inhabited, and its land area is 2,281 sq km. The capital is Naha, on [[Okinawa Island]]. The Ryukyu Kingdom was incorporated into Japan as the prefecture in 1879. After the [[Battle of Okinawa]] in 1945, the islands were under U.S. administration until 1972. Around 70% of the land exclusively used by U.S. forces in Japan is here. The islands are the birthplace of [[Karate|karate]].

Landlocked U.S. state in the South Central region. Its capital and largest city is [[Oklahoma City]]. The name derives from the Choctaw words *okla*, meaning people, and *humma*, meaning red. The state is the 20th-most extensive and 28th-most populous, and it is nicknamed the Sooner State. Most of the state lies in the Great Plains, Cross Timbers and Interior Highlands, all regions prone to severe weather. A major producer of [[Natural gas|natural gas]], oil and [[Agriculture|agricultural]] products, it relies on aviation, energy, telecommunications and biotechnology. According to the 2020 census, 14.2% of Oklahomans identify as American Indians, the highest share of any state.

Capital and most populous city of [[Oklahoma]], U.S. (pop., 2020: 681,054). It is the county seat of Oklahoma County and has one of the world's largest livestock markets. Oil, natural gas and related industries form its largest economic sector, and the city sits in the middle of an active oil field. Tinker Air Force Base is a major federal employer. The city was founded during the Land Run of 1889 and grew to more than 10,000 people within hours. It has been struck by 13 violent [[Tornado|tornadoes]] since records began in 1890. The metropolitan area had an estimated 1.49 million residents.

Domestic terrorist attack in [[Oklahoma City]] on April 19, 1995. Anti-government extremist [[Timothy McVeigh|Timothy McVeigh]], assisted by Terry Nichols, detonated a truck bomb in front of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building. The blast killed 168 people, including a rescue worker who died from falling debris, and injured 684. McVeigh was executed by [[Lethal injection|lethal injection]] on June 11, 2001, after being convicted in 1997. Nichols received [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] without parole. McVeigh and Nichols were motivated by anger at federal handling of the Ruby Ridge and [[Waco siege|Waco]] sieges. The bombing remains the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history.

Flowering plant of the mallow family, grown for its edible pods. Known as lady's fingers in some English-speaking countries, *Abelmoschus esculentus* is a perennial often grown as an annual, reaching about 2 meters tall. It is related to [[Cotton|cotton]] and [[Hibiscus|hibiscus]]. The fruit is a ribbed capsule up to 18 cm long, and pods must be harvested while immature, usually within a week of pollination, before they become fibrous. Okra originated in Ethiopia, Eritrea and eastern Sudan and spread around the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]]. Ships in the [[Atlantic slave trade|Atlantic slave trade]] introduced it to the Americas, and its presence was recorded in Brazil by 1658. It was common throughout the [[Southern United States|Southern United States]] by 1800. It is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant vegetables, and it features in dishes such as [[Gumbo|gumbo]]. Global production exceeds 11 million metric tons a year, led by India.

World's largest folk festival, held in [[Munich]]. It combines a beer festival with amusement rides, games and food stalls. It runs from mid-September to the first Sunday in October on the Theresienwiese, and attendance reached a record 7.2 million in 2023, when visitors drank about 7.4 million liters of beer. The first festival, on October 12, 1810, celebrated the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig of [[Bavaria]] and Princess Therese of Saxony-Hildburghausen, and it included a horse race. The festival has since been canceled several times, including for cholera epidemics, the [[Austro-Prussian War]] in 1866, and during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021.

Russian religious dissenters preserving pre-reform Orthodox liturgy. They reject the liturgical reforms of [[Patriarch Nikon of Moscow]], enacted between 1653 and 1656 and condemned in 1667. Under [[Catherine the Great]] they gained near-complete tolerance, but persecution resumed under Nicholas I. Full religious freedom came only after the [[Russian Revolution of 1905]]. Stalin-era persecution decimated the communities. The main division is between the popovtsy, who were willing to employ priests from the state church, and the priestless bezpopovtsy. In the early 21st century there were over 1 million Old Believers, mostly in Russia, [[Latvia]], [[Lithuania]], [[Romania]] and the [[United States]].

First kingdom on the Korean Peninsula, also known as Gojoseon. According to the *Samguk yusa*, it was founded in 2333 BC by the legendary Tan'gun, a date celebrated in North and South Korea as Gaecheonjeol. Historians regard Tan'gun as mythical, though some see the legend as reflecting early social conditions. The kingdom had the most advanced culture on the peninsula, and its capital was Wanggeom-seong, now [[Pyongyang]], from at least the 2nd century BC. The Go prefix, meaning old, distinguishes it from the [[Joseon]] founded in 1392. In 194 BC the ruling dynasty was overthrown by Wiman, a refugee from the [[Han dynasty|Han]] vassal state of Yan. In 108 BC the Han dynasty under Emperor Wu conquered Wiman Joseon and set up four commanderies. The area was conquered by Goguryeo in AD 313.

Earliest attested form of the English language, also called Anglo-Saxon. It developed from the Germanic dialects of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes, who settled in Britain in the mid-5th century and displaced the Celtic Common Brittonic and the Latin of Roman Britain. Old English had four main dialects: Kentish, Mercian, Northumbrian and West Saxon, the last forming the basis of the literary standard. Its grammar had many inflections, and it is largely incomprehensible to modern English speakers without study. After the [[Norman Conquest]] of 1066, Anglo-Norman replaced English among the upper classes, and the language developed into [[Middle English]]. Around 85% of Old English words are no longer in use, but the survivors form the basic vocabulary of [[Modern English]]. Its literature includes the epic poem *Beowulf*.

Period of ancient Egyptian history, c. 2686–2181 BC. Also called the Age of the Pyramids, it includes the reigns of Fourth Dynasty builders such as Sneferu, under whom [[Pyramid|pyramid]] building was perfected, and of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, who commissioned the [[Great Pyramid of Giza|pyramids at Giza]]. Djoser, first king of the Third Dynasty, ordered the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by his architect [[Imhotep]]. The king was regarded as a living god who ruled absolutely. The period ended in disunity, the First Intermediate Period, after droughts, provincial autonomy and the long reign of Pepi II weakened central authority. It is one of three so-called golden ages, a concept coined in 1845 by the German Egyptologist Baron von Bunsen.

[[Polytheism|Polytheistic]] religion of the North Germanic peoples before Christianization. It was a branch of [[Germanic paganism|Germanic religion]] and was replaced by Christianity, although elements persisted in folklore. Its deities were divided into the Æsir and Vanir, and the most widespread were [[Odin|Odin]] and [[Thor|Thor]]. Cosmology centered on the world tree [[Yggdrasil|Yggdrasil]], with realms such as Midgard, where humans live. The religion was transmitted orally and focused on ritual, with kings and chiefs performing public sacrifices. Practitioners of seiðr, a form of sorcery some scholars describe as shamanistic, existed. The dead were buried or cremated, typically with grave goods. Academic study began in the early 19th century, influenced by [[Romanticism|Romanticism]]. Knowledge comes from archaeology, runic inscriptions and 13th-century works that record Norse mythology.

First division of the Christian Bible, based mainly on the [[Hebrew Bible]]. It draws on the 24 books of the Tanakh, written mainly in Hebrew with some [[Aramaic|Aramaic]], but its order and contents differ from the Jewish canon. Protestant Bibles typically have 39 books, Catholic canons 46, and Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches up to 49. Books outside the Hebrew canon, called deuterocanonical, mostly come from the [[Septuagint|Septuagint]], an ancient Greek translation. Christians traditionally divide the text into the Pentateuch, or [[Torah|Torah]], historical books, poetic books and prophetic books. Christian interpretation often reads it in light of the [[New Testament|New Testament]], while Jewish interpretation does not regard it as an old covenant superseded by a new one. Scholars debate the historicity of the patriarchs, the Exodus and the United Monarchy, and mainstream scholarship takes a skeptical but balanced approach to material from the 9th century BC onward.

Family of small [[Passerine|passerine]] birds restricted to the Old World. The family Muscicapidae includes 357 species in 57 genera. Most are small arboreal insectivores that often catch prey on the wing. Apart from several vagrants, two species, the bluethroat and northern wheatear, also occur in North America. The family name, from Latin for fly and to catch, was introduced in 1822 by the Scottish naturalist John Fleming. Broad groupings that once included [[Thrush (bird)|thrushes]] were split after DNA studies showed that their subfamilies were not closely related. In 1998 the American Ornithologists' Union treated thrushes as a separate family, and most authors have followed.

[[Primate|Primate]] family of 24 genera and 139 species, native to Africa and Asia. Old World monkeys are the largest primate family, including [[Baboon|baboons]], [[Macaque|macaques]], colobus monkeys and [[Mandrill|mandrills]]. They are more closely related to [[Ape|apes]] than to [[New World monkey|New World monkeys]], and the two groups diverged from a common ancestor 25 million to 30 million years ago. The smallest is the Angolan talapoin, and the largest is the male mandrill, about 70 cm long and up to 50 kg. Some, such as colobus monkeys, are arboreal, while baboons are terrestrial. Most are at least partly omnivorous, but plant matter forms the bulk of their diet. They live in [[Rainforest|rain forests]], [[Savanna|savannas]] and mountainous terrain, and once inhabited much of Europe. Two subfamilies are recognized: the mainly African Cercopithecinae and the Colobinae, which includes most Asian genera.

Family of small [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, also called true sparrows. The family Passeridae is distinct from the New World sparrows of the family Passerellidae. Most species are small, plump, brown and gray birds with short tails and stubby, powerful beaks. They are primarily seed-eaters that also consume small insects. Many species nest on buildings, and the [[House sparrow|house sparrow]] and Eurasian tree sparrow thrive in cities in large numbers. The family includes the genus Passer, snowfinches (Montifringilla) and rock sparrows (Petronia). It was introduced in 1815 by the French [[Polymath|polymath]] Constantine Samuel Rafinesque. Some earlier classifications included the estrildid finches, which are now usually placed in their own family, Estrildidae.
